problem: “the North American Native” is awkward and unidiomatic after the renderer’s own Native American convention.
replacement: If the Native American tribes that now live in the heart of the continent could summon up enough energy to try to civilize themselves, they might possibly succeed. Already superior to the barbarous nations around them, they would gradually gain strength and experience. When the Europeans appeared on their borders, they would be in a position, if not to maintain their independence, at least to assert their right to the soil and to merge with the conquerors. But the misfortune of the Native Americans is that they have come into contact with a civilized people that is also (it must be admitted) the most avaricious nation on the globe, while they are still semi-barbarous. They find despots in their teachers, and they receive knowledge from the hand of oppression. Living in the freedom of the woods, the Native American of North America was poor, but he felt inferior to no one. As soon as he wants to enter the social scale of the whites, however, he takes the lowest rank in society, for he enters the circle of science and wealth ignorant and poor. He has led a life of agitation, beset with evils and dangers but filled at the same time with proud emotions. *r Now he is obliged to submit to a wearisome, obscure, and degraded state, and to earn the bread that feeds him by hard and ignoble labor. In his eyes these are the only results civilization can boast of, and even this much he is not sure to obtain.

problem: Source says the destructive influence of highly civilized nations upon less civilized ones has been exemplified by Europeans; candidate turns it into a modal claim (“can destroy”) and drops the idea of influence.
replacement: s [ The Europeans themselves have shown how destructive the influence of highly civilized nations can be upon less civilized ones. About a century ago the French founded the town of Vincennes on the Wabash, in the middle of the wilderness, and lived there in great plenty until the American settlers arrived. The Americans first ruined the earlier inhabitants through competition and then bought their lands at a very low price. When M. de Volney, from whom I borrow these details, passed through Vincennes, the number of the French was reduced to a hundred individuals, most of whom were about to move to Louisiana or to Canada. These French settlers were worthy people, but idle and uneducated; they had picked up many of the habits of savages. The Americans, who were perhaps their inferiors from a moral point of view, were immeasurably superior to them in intelligence: they were industrious, well informed, rich, and used to governing their own community.

problem: “extirpation” rendered “extermination”, which sharpens the force (source means destruction of a few tribes, not necessarily killing of all members).
replacement: If we consider the tyrannical measures adopted by the legislatures of the Southern States, the conduct of their Governors, and the decrees of their courts of justice, we shall be convinced that the final aim of their policy is the complete expulsion of the Native Americans. The Americans of that part of the Union look on the aborigines with jealousy. *v They know that these tribes have not yet lost the traditions of savage life, and before civilization has fixed them permanently to the soil, they intend to force them to withdraw by driving them to despair. The Creeks and Cherokees, oppressed by the several States, have appealed to the central government. It is by no means indifferent to their misfortunes and sincerely wants to save the remnant of the natives and keep them in free possession of the territory that the Union is pledged to respect. *w But the several States offer such formidable resistance to carrying out this plan that the government is obliged to consent to the destruction of a few barbarous tribes, so as not to endanger the safety of the American Union.

problem: Typography: unspaced em dash inside the Cherokee petition (“seen—a few”) not converted to spaced em dash, inconsistent with 19:83 and 19:84.
replacement: Thus the tyranny of the States forces the savages to retire, and the Union, by its promises and resources, makes their retreat easier. These measures tend to precisely the same end. *z “By the will of our Father in Heaven, the Governor of the whole world,” said the Cherokees in their petition to Congress, *a “the red man of America has become small, and the white man great and renowned. When the ancestors of the people of these United States first came to the shores of America they found the red man strong: though he was ignorant and savage, yet he received them kindly, and gave them dry land to rest their weary feet. They met in peace, and shook hands in token of friendship. Whatever the white man wanted and asked of the Indian, the latter willingly gave. At that time the Indian was the lord, and the white man the suppliant. But now the scene has changed. The strength of the red man has become weakness. As his neighbors increased in numbers his power became less and less, and now, of the many and powerful tribes who once covered these United States, only a few are to be seen — a few whom a sweeping pestilence has left. The northern tribes, who were once so numerous and powerful, are now nearly extinct. Thus it has happened to the red man of America. Shall we, who are remnants, share the same fate?”

problem: Typography: unspaced em dash in “treaty:—‘The” not converted to a spaced em dash.
replacement: “The land on which we stand we have received as an inheritance from our fathers, who possessed it from time immemorial, as a gift from our common Father in Heaven. They bequeathed it to us as their children, and we have sacredly kept it, as containing the remains of our beloved men. This right of inheritance we have never ceded nor ever forfeited. Permit us to ask what better right can the people have to a country than the right of inheritance and immemorial peaceable possession? We know it is said of late by the State of Georgia and by the Executive of the United States, that we have forfeited this right; but we think this is said gratuitously. At what time have we made the forfeit? What great crime have we committed, whereby we must forever be divested of our country and rights? Was it when we were hostile to the United States, and took part with the King of Great Britain, during the struggle for independence? If so, why was not this forfeiture declared in the first treaty of peace between the United States and our beloved men? Why was not such an article as the following inserted in the treaty: — ‘The United States give peace to the Cherokees, but, for the part they took in the late war, declare them to be but tenants at will, to be removed when the convenience of the States, within whose chartered limits they live, shall require it’? That was the proper time to assume such a possession. But it was not thought of, nor would our forefathers have agreed to any treaty whose tendency was to deprive them of their rights and their country.”

problem: “eternal mark of his ignominy” softened to “lasting mark of his disgrace”; Tocqueville’s force is eternal.
replacement: The greatest difficulty in antiquity was changing the law; among the moderns it is changing the customs. And as far as we are concerned, the real obstacles begin where those of the ancients ended. This comes from the fact that, among the moderns, the abstract and transient fact of slavery is fatally joined to the physical and permanent fact of color. The tradition of slavery dishonors the race, and the distinctiveness of the race keeps the tradition of slavery alive. No African has ever voluntarily emigrated to the shores of the New World, and from this it must be inferred that all the Black people now found in that hemisphere are either slaves or freedmen. Thus the Black person passes the eternal mark of his disgrace on to all his descendants, and although the law may abolish slavery, God alone can erase the traces of its existence.
